posts.title: Public interface connected to the Internal Market Information System for the declaration of posting of workers
posts.label: ✅ Adopted — Council gave the final green light
posts.summaryLabel: Legislative Observatory, Decision by Parliament, 1st reading
posts.whatsNext: Signature by the Parliament and Council presidents, then publication in the Official Journal. It enters into force on the date the act sets — by default the 20th day after publication.

aiSummaries.text:
The European Parliament approved a regulation, by 558 votes to 93 with 18 abstentions, that creates a free, multilingual online system for companies to declare when they send workers to work in another EU country. The system is linked to the existing Internal Market Information System. Its aims are to make it easier for service providers to operate across borders, cut down on paperwork, and help national authorities check that rules protecting posted workers are followed.

Service providers can use the system to set up a secure account, create and submit posting declarations, check and manage their details, and upload supporting documents once a declaration has been submitted. Every change made by a user is recorded. Workers receive an electronic copy of the parts of the declaration that concern them, along with a link to the official national website giving information on pay and working conditions. The authorities of the host country and the company's home country can see the submitted information and exchange messages with service providers.

Member States that choose to use the system must tell the Commission at least six months in advance. They may not add extra requirements for companies that file through it. Where national law requires it, the system can also accept declarations from companies based outside the EU that send workers into a Member State, so that those firms are not treated more favourably than EU-based ones.

The online form asks for information needed for workplace inspections. This covers the service provider and its legal representative, the posted workers and their number, tasks and indicative hourly pay, the details of the assignment such as dates, type of work, working conditions and any shared accommodation, contact people in the host country and the social partners, and the client receiving the service. For non-EU workers, it also asks for their residence and work permits, or other proof of lawful stay or employment, and the start and, if relevant, end dates of their employment.

The Commission is treated as the controller of the personal data. Information and documents must be kept in the system for up to 36 months after the posting ends, so they can be reused in later declarations. The European Labour Authority will receive statistics drawn from the declarations submitted.

posts.title: Transport: enforcement of passenger rights in the Union
posts.label: ✅ Adopted — Council gave the final green light
posts.summary:
The European Parliament adopted by 652 votes to 2, with 8 abstentions, a legislative resolution on the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Regulations (EC) No 261/2004, (EC) No 1107/2006, (EU) No 1177/2010, (EU) No 181/2011 and (EU) 2021/782 as regards enforcement of passenger rights in the Union.
The European Parliament adopted its position at first reading by amending the proposal as follows:
Reimbursement by air travel intermediaries
The amended text clarifies the rules on reimbursement in the case of cancellations when flights are booked via an intermediary, such as travel agents or online booking platforms.
The intermediary must inform the passenger, in a clear, comprehensible, and easily accessible manner, whether the airline agrees to process the refund through the intermediary, and what the refund procedure will be. Processing the refund through the intermediary is free for the passenger. Before a passenger finalises a booking, the intermediary must inform them of any applicable intermediation, administrative, service, or cancellation fees, as well as the passenger's right to a full refund of the intermediation fees.
When a passenger has booked a ticket through an intermediary, the airline may process the refund through that intermediary, in which case the intermediary will reimburse the passenger. If the intermediary is not involved in the refund or did not use their own account to purchase the tickets, the airline will reimburse the passenger directly within seven calendar days of the passenger providing proof of the total ticket price and any intermediary fees paid, as well as the passenger's payment details.
If a refund is obtained through intermediaries who used their own accounts to purchase tickets from an airline, the airline must reimburse the intermediary within seven calendar days of the passenger's choice of refund method. The intermediary then refunds the passenger the full ticket price and any applicable intermediary fees within a further seven days , using the same payment method, and provides details of the refund. If the airline does not receive confirmation of payment from the intermediary within 14 days , it must contact the passenger no later than the following day. Upon receipt of the required data and supporting documentation, the airline will issue a direct refund to the passenger within seven calendar days and notify the intermediary.
Common form for compensation and reimbursement claims
The Commission will adopt an implementing act establishing a common form for compensation and reimbursement. These common forms will be available on the European Commission's website, in all European languages ​​and for all types of transport . Carriers may not reject any claim on the grounds that the passenger did not use the common form, or that the passenger submitted the form by means other than electronic means.
Designation of national enforcement bodies
Each Member State will designate one or more national bodies responsible for enforcing the regulation. These bodies will closely monitor compliance with the regulation and take the necessary measures to ensure respect for passengers' rights. Monitoring activities may include audits, inspections, interviews, and the examination of documents .
Member States will each designate a body for passenger complaints . The body for passenger complaints will acknowledge receipt of the complaint within 14 calendar days of receiving it.
Information about suspected practices of non-compliance
The Commission may alert the national enforcement bodies about specific suspected practices of non-compliance by one or more carriers, terminal operators, port authorities, travel agents, ticket vendors or tour operators. Where the national enforcement body initiates any investigation, it will inform the Commission, upon request, of its findings.
Improved rights for vulnerable passengers
An air carrier may require that a person with disabilities or person with reduced mobility should be able to travel accompanied by another person who is capable of providing the assistance required. Where the air carrier introduces such a requirement but cannot provide the assistance needed by the disabled person or person with reduced mobility, that person should be allowed to travel accompanied by another person of their choice , who should travel free of charge and be seated next to that disabled person or person with reduced mobility.
Furthermore, upon request, a station manager, a railway undertaking, a ticket vendor or a tour operator will provide persons with disabilities and persons with reduced mobility with information, including in an accessible format, on the accessibility of the station and associated facilities , and of rail services and on the access conditions of rolling stock and inform persons with disabilities and persons with reduced mobility about facilities on board.
A recognised assistance dog will be permitted to accompany them.
Where railway undertakings or station managers cause the loss of, or damage to, mobility equipment , including wheelchairs, or the loss of, or injury to, recognised assistance dogs used by persons with disabilities or persons with reduced mobility, they will be liable and will provide compensation without undue delay.
Review of service quality standards
By five years from the date of entry into force of this amending Regulation, the Commission will carry out a comprehensive evaluation of all service quality standards, as part of the first report on the operation and the effects of this Regulation.

aiSummaries.text:
This measure strengthens passenger rights when travelling by air and rail, with a focus on refunds, enforcement, and support for people with disabilities or reduced mobility. The European Parliament adopted the proposal by 652 votes to 2, with 8 abstentions, at first reading, after amending the original proposal.

When a flight is booked through an intermediary, such as a travel agent or online platform, the intermediary must clearly tell the passenger whether the airline will handle the refund through them and how the refund will work. Using the intermediary for the refund is free for the passenger. Before a booking is finalised, the intermediary must also disclose any fees that apply, and tell the passenger they have a right to a full refund of intermediation fees. If the airline refunds through the intermediary, the intermediary pays the passenger back. If not, the airline pays the passenger directly within seven calendar days of receiving proof of the total ticket price and any intermediary fees, along with the passenger's payment details. Where an intermediary bought the tickets using its own account, the airline must repay the intermediary within seven calendar days of the passenger choosing a refund method. The intermediary then has a further seven days to repay the passenger in full, including any intermediary fees, and to provide details of the refund. If the airline has not received confirmation of that payment within 14 days, it must contact the passenger by the following day, and it can then pay the passenger directly within seven calendar days.

The Commission will set up a common form for compensation and reimbursement claims, available on its website in all European languages and for all types of transport. Carriers cannot reject a claim just because the passenger did not use this form or sent it by a non-electronic method.

Each Member State will appoint one or more national bodies to enforce the regulation, monitor compliance closely, and take the steps needed to protect passengers' rights. Their work may include audits, inspections, interviews, and document checks. Each Member State will also designate a body to handle passenger complaints, which must confirm receipt of a complaint within 14 calendar days. The Commission can alert national bodies to suspected non-compliance by carriers, terminal operators, port authorities, travel agents, ticket vendors or tour operators, and if a national body investigates, it must share its findings with the Commission on request.

Passengers with disabilities or reduced mobility get stronger protections. An airline may require such a passenger to travel with a companion who can provide the help they need. If the airline requires this but cannot itself provide the needed assistance, the passenger may travel with a companion of their choice, who travels free of charge and sits next to them. On request, station managers, railway undertakings, ticket vendors and tour operators must give information, including in accessible formats, about station and rail accessibility and onboard facilities. Recognised assistance dogs are allowed to accompany these passengers. If railway undertakings or station managers lose or damage mobility equipment, such as wheelchairs, or harm a recognised assistance dog, they are liable and must pay compensation without undue delay.

Within five years of the regulation entering into force, the Commission will carry out a full review of all service quality standards, as part of its first report on how the regulation works and what effects it has.

posts.title: 'AgoraEU' programme 2028–2034
posts.label: 🗳️ Lead committee adopted its report
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to establish the 'AgoraEU' programme for the period 2028-2034.
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: on 16 July 2025, the European Commission unveiled its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034 , a EUR 2 trillion budget designed to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, competitiveness, and resilience. This new MFF will significantly enhance the EU's capacity to deliver on core policies while addressing new and emerging priorities.
The 2028-2034 MFF proposal aims at addressing ‘complexities, weaknesses and rigidities’ currently present in the EU’s budget, and provides a framework that is more focused, simpler, with fewer and more impactful programmes. For this reason, and to increase the budget’s flexibility and ability to respond to changing realities and emerging problems, this proposal seeks to streamline the EU intervention in the areas of culture, media and equality, citizens, rights and values, exploiting connections and synergies where relevant, while respecting the singularity and specific needs of each of these policy areas.
The Programme should succeed the Creative Europe Programme established by Regulation (EU) 2021/818 of the European Parliament and the Council and the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values Programme, established by Regulation (EU) 2021/692 of the European Parliament and of the Council. It should streamline various funding actions in support of media freedom and pluralism, fight against disinformation in support of the provision on information on Union affairs.
CONTENT: the proposed regulation establishes the AgoraEU Programme for the period 2028-2034. A financial envelope for the implementation of the Programme for the period 2028-2034 is set at EUR 8 582 000 000 .
Its main objectives are to:
- promote cultural and linguistic diversity and heritage;
- increase the competitiveness of the cultural and creative sectors, in particular the media and audiovisual industries, to safeguard artistic and media freedom, and to protect and promote equality, active citizenship, rights and values as enshrined in the Treaties and in the Charter, thereby enhancing democratic participation and societal resilience within the Union.
Within this general objective, the Programme will have three separate strands implementing the following specific objectives:
Creative Europe - Culture strand will:
- contribute to cross-border cultural creation, cooperation, participation and accessibility, and cross-border circulation of a diversity of cultural works, while strengthening the social, economic and international dimensions of the cultural and creative sectors (‘culture’).
MEDIA+ strand will:
- contribute to the cultural diversity and competitiveness of the audiovisual and video games industries, notably by enhancing creation and cross-border distribution of European content and its access by citizens (‘audiovisual’);
- contribute to a free, viable and diverse Union information ecosystem, notably by supporting free and independent journalism and news media, enhancing citizens’ access to trustworthy information and tackling disinformation (‘news’).
Democracy, Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (‘CERV+’) strand will:
- contribute to protecting and promoting fundamental rights, equality and non-discrimination and Union citizen’s rights enshrined in the Treaties including free movement of citizens, and empowering civil society (‘rights, equality, citizens and civil society’);
- contribute to fighting against gender-based violence, violence against children and other groups at risk of such violence (‘Daphne’);
- contribute to enhancing democratic participation and upholding the rule of law (‘democratic participation and rule of law’).
The EU should promote synergies among the media, culture, and civic spheres, bringing together public and private entities as well as promoting cross-sectoral cooperation, and innovation, to address common challenges and contribute to societal resilience and democratic participation.

aiSummaries.text:
The European Commission has proposed a new EU programme called AgoraEU to run from 2028 to 2034. It would replace the current Creative Europe and Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values programmes, and it is meant to bring several funding efforts together into one simpler framework. The European Parliament would decide on it through the ordinary legislative procedure, on an equal footing with the Council.

The proposal sits within a broader EU budget plan for 2028 to 2034, which the Commission unveiled on 16 July 2025. That plan totals EUR 2 trillion and aims to make the EU's spending more focused, simpler and more flexible. The aim is to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, competitiveness and resilience, and to respond to new problems as they arise.

AgoraEU would have a financial envelope of EUR 8,582,000,000 for 2028 to 2034. Its overall goals are to promote cultural and linguistic diversity and heritage, to strengthen the competitiveness of the cultural and creative sectors, especially media and audiovisual industries, and to protect artistic and media freedom. It also aims to protect and promote equality, active citizenship, rights and values, which should support democratic participation and resilience across the Union.

The programme has three strands. The Culture strand would support cross-border creation, cooperation and access to cultural works, and strengthen the social, economic and international side of the cultural and creative sectors. The MEDIA+ strand would support the audiovisual and video games industries, including the creation and cross-border distribution of European content, and would also support a free, viable and diverse information ecosystem. This includes backing independent journalism and news media, helping citizens access trustworthy information, and tackling disinformation. The third strand, CERV+, would protect fundamental rights, equality, non-discrimination and citizens' rights such as free movement, and empower civil society. It would also fight gender-based violence and violence against children and other at-risk groups, and promote democratic participation and the rule of law.

Finally, the EU would encourage links between the media, culture and civic spheres, bringing together public and private bodies and supporting cooperation and innovation across sectors. The goal is to tackle shared challenges and strengthen societal resilience and democratic participation.

posts.title: Union support for the Schengen area, for European integrated border management and for the common policy on visas 2028–2034
posts.label: 🗳️ Lead committee adopted its report
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to establish the Union's support for the Schengen area, European integrated border management and the common policy on visas for the period 2028-2034.
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: on 16 July 2025, the Commission unveiled its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034 (MFF), a budget of nearly EUR 2 trillion between 2028 and 2034 designed to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, competitiveness and resilience.
In this context, this proposal, together with the proposal for a regulation establishing Union support for asylum, migration and integration and the proposal for a regulation establishing Union support for internal security , provide the specific legal framework for Union action in the areas of integrated management of Europe's external borders, the smooth functioning of the Schengen area and European visa policy, and the efficient management of migration flows and internal security for the period from 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2034.
In order to ensure the effective and efficient functioning of the Schengen area without internal borders , it is essential to have a strong governance framework, effective integrated European border management and EU visa policy to ensure the integrity and resilience of the Schengen area. It is therefore appropriate to support the efforts of Member States to protect the Union's external borders, to combat illegal border crossings and unauthorised movements between Member States, as well as to modernise and improve the overall efficiency of visa processing and prevent abuse of visa policy.
The proposal aims to address the need for greater flexibility in the management of Union support, including a stronger performance orientation, as well as increased simplification for all actors involved in its implementation.
CONTENT: the proposed regulation sets out the objectives and financing of Union support for integrated European border management and European visa policy for the period from 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2034 .
Budget
The indicative financial envelope for the implementation of the objectives under Union support is set at EUR 15 396 750 000 in current prices for the period 2028-2034 . This Union support will be provided under the horizontal rules of the European Fund for Economic, Social and Territorial Cohesion, Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Fisheries and Maritime Affairs, Prosperity and Security.
Objectives for Union support
In order to ensure a strong and efficient European integrated management of external borders, the smooth functioning of the Schengen area and the effectiveness of visa policy, Union support will contribute to the achievement of each of the following objectives:
- support the effective implementation, application and development of the Schengen framework and strengthen the governance, integrity and security of the Schengen area without internal borders;
- support effective integrated European management of external borders , implemented as a shared responsibility between the European Border and Coast Guard Agency and national border management authorities, using new technologies to facilitate legitimate border crossings, combat illegal immigration, cross-border crime and the instrumentalisation of migration, and promote effective returns;
- support a harmonised approach to the timely issuance of visas and facilitate legitimate travel, while preventing migration and security risks.
Member States should ensure that the priorities of their National and Regional Partnership Plans include actions to achieve each of the objectives of the Union support under this Regulation, and, that the allocation of resources between objectives is proportionate to the identified challenges and needs.
The proposal includes provisions for financing EU aid, provisions for Schengen Associated Countries, and provisions for implementing the special transit scheme in Lithuania. Up to EUR 450 million will be allocated to Lithuania's National and Regional Partnership Plan to assist Lithuania in managing the transit of people between the Kaliningrad region and other parts of the Russian Federation.
The proposed regulation also lays down rules on the budgetary treatment of resources intended for the operating costs of the European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS) and rules on the budgetary treatment of financial contributions from Member States for the purposes of the annual solidarity pool established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1351 of the European Parliament and of the Council.

aiSummaries.text:
The measure sets out how the EU will support its shared border and visa system from 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2034. The aim is to keep the Schengen area, the zone without internal border checks, working well and secure, to manage the EU's external borders together, and to issue visas in a consistent way that makes legitimate travel easy while guarding against migration and security risks. The proposal is a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council, so Parliament decides it through the ordinary legislative procedure on an equal footing with the Council.

The proposal sits within the EU's next long-term budget for 2028 to 2034, which the Commission described in July 2025 as nearly EUR 2 trillion. It works alongside separate proposals on asylum, migration and integration, and on internal security. The rationale is that the Schengen area depends on strong governance, effective border management and a sound visa policy. The proposal also aims to give more flexibility in how support is managed, with a stronger focus on performance and simpler procedures for everyone involved.

The indicative budget for this support is EUR 15,396,750,000 in current prices for 2028 to 2034. The money comes through the horizontal rules of a single EU fund covering cohesion, agriculture and rural affairs, fisheries and maritime affairs, prosperity and security.

Support has three objectives. The first is to implement and develop the Schengen rules and strengthen the area's governance, integrity and security. The second is to run integrated management of the external borders as a shared responsibility between the European Border and Coast Guard Agency and national authorities, using new technologies to ease legitimate crossings, fight illegal immigration and cross-border crime, and promote effective returns. The third is to harmonise visa issuing so it is timely and makes legitimate travel easier, while preventing migration and security risks. Member States must include actions for each objective in their national and regional partnership plans, with resources matched to the challenges and needs identified.

The proposal also covers support for Schengen associated countries and a special transit scheme in Lithuania. Up to EUR 450 million will go to Lithuania's partnership plan to help it manage the transit of people between the Kaliningrad region and the rest of the Russian Federation. Finally, it sets budget rules for running costs of the European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS) and for Member States' financial contributions to the annual solidarity pool established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1351.

posts.title: Union support for asylum, migration and integration 2028–2034
posts.label: 🗳️ Lead committee adopted its report
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to establish Union support for asylum, migration and integration for the period 2028-2034.
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: on 16 July 2025, the Commission unveiled its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034 , a budget of nearly EUR 2 trillion between 2028 and 2034 designed to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, competitiveness and resilience.
In this context, this proposal, together with the proposal for a regulation establishing Union support for the Schengen area, European integrated border management and the common visa policy , and the proposal for a regulation establishing Union support for internal security , provide the specific legal framework for Union action in the areas of effective migration management and asylum for the period from 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2034.
The Pact on Migration and Asylum establishes a comprehensive approach to asylum, migration, and border management, based on solidarity and fair responsibility-sharing among Member States. Its success depends on collective commitment, with each Member State required to develop a national plan in line with the Commission's Common Implementation Plan. Implementation requires national reforms and significant financial resources supported by EU funds.
The scope of Union assistance should be coherent with political priorities and flexible, so as to allow for new developments to be taken into account. This proposal aims to address the need for greater flexibility in the management of Union support, including a stronger performance orientation, as well as increased simplification for all actors involved in its implementation.
CONTENT: the proposed regulation sets out the objectives and financing of Union support for the implementation, strengthening and development of the common asylum policy and the common immigration policy for the period from 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2034. The Union support will contribute to the efficient management of migration flows and asylum, including by providing support for the implementation, strengthening and development of the Pact on Migration and Asylum, and the common system of temporary protection for displaced persons in the event of a mass influx.
Financing
The indicative financial envelope for the implementation of the objectives under Union support is set at EUR 11 975 428 500 in current prices for the period 2028-2034 . This Union support will be provided under the horizontal rules of the European Fund for Economic, Social and Territorial Cohesion, Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Fisheries and Maritime Affairs, Prosperity and Security.
Support for asylum, migration and integration
In order to ensure efficient management of migration flows, Union support will contribute to each of the following objectives:
- strengthen and develop all aspects of the Common European Asylum System;
- enhance effective, safe and dignified return and readmission , promote and contribute to effective reintegration in third countries, and contribute to the fight against irregular migration by preventing and combating migrant smuggling and trafficking in human beings, as well as the instrumentalisation of irregular migration;
- strengthen and develop legal migration to Member States according to their needs, and promote and contribute to the effective integration and social inclusion of third-country nationals during the early phases of settlement;
- ensure solidarity and fair sharing of responsibilities between Member States, including through practical cooperation, innovative methods and new technologies.
Member States should ensure that the priorities of their national and regional partnership plans include actions to achieve each of the objectives of Union support under the Regulation and that the allocation of resources between the objectives is proportionate to the challenges and needs identified.
Resettlement, humanitarian admission and transfer of applicants for international protection
A Member State will receive, in addition to their allocation:
- an amount of EUR 10 000 for each person admitted under resettlement;
- an amount of EUR 6 000 for each person admitted through humanitarian admission, this amount being able to be increased to EUR 8 000 for persons belonging to one or more vulnerable groups: women and children at risk, minors, persons with medical needs that can only be met through humanitarian admission;
- an additional amount of EUR 10 000 (i) per applicant for international protection for whom that Member State becomes responsible following relocation; (ii) per beneficiary of international protection relocated to that Member State. These amounts will be increased to EUR 12 000 for each applicant for international protection or beneficiary of international protection, respectively, who is an unaccompanied minor relocated to that Member State.
Union support will be provided to the activities and future development of the European Migration Network.

aiSummaries.text:
This proposed EU regulation sets out how the Union will support asylum, migration and integration from 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2034. It is meant to help countries carry out and build on the EU's Pact on Migration and Asylum, along with a system for temporary protection of displaced people during a sudden large influx. The European Parliament and the Council would decide on it together, as equal partners.

The proposal comes as part of the Commission's plan for the EU's next long-term budget, which is nearly EUR 2 trillion for 2028 to 2034. It works alongside related proposals on border management and internal security. The Pact asks every Member State to develop a national plan, and carrying these out requires national reforms and significant money, much of which comes from EU funds.

The regulation has four main goals. The first is to strengthen all parts of the common asylum system. The second is to make returns and readmission safe and dignified, help people reintegrate in their home countries, and fight irregular migration, including smuggling, trafficking and the use of irregular migration as a tool. The third is to expand legal migration in line with each country's needs and help third-country nationals integrate and join society in the early stages after arriving. The fourth is to share responsibilities fairly among Member States, using practical cooperation, new methods and new technologies.

The indicative budget for these goals is EUR 11,975,428,500 in current prices for 2028 to 2034. The money will be provided under the shared rules of the European Fund for Economic, Social and Territorial Cohesion, Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Fisheries and Maritime Affairs, Prosperity and Security. Member States must make sure their national and regional plans include actions for each goal, with resources divided in proportion to the challenges and needs they identify.

Countries also receive extra payments on top of their regular allocation. They get EUR 10,000 for each person admitted through resettlement and EUR 6,000 for each person admitted through humanitarian admission, which can rise to EUR 8,000 for people in certain vulnerable groups. For relocation, they get an additional EUR 10,000 for each applicant or beneficiary of international protection relocated to them, rising to EUR 12,000 for unaccompanied minors. Finally, the regulation provides support for the European Migration Network's activities and future development.

aiSummaries.text:
The EU Space Act is a proposed regulation that would set common rules for space activities across the European Union. Its aim is to make it easier for companies to access the market, to improve safety in space, and to create a fair and predictable environment for businesses.

Right now, 13 Member States have passed their own national space laws, and more are planning to do so. These different approaches create a patchwork of rules that fragments the single market and can make it harder for space companies to provide data and services across borders. The European Commission's political guidelines for 2024-2029 and the Draghi report both identify space as a key strategic sector and call for a common EU legal framework in the short term.

The proposal would create an EU legal framework for space-based data and services provided by EU space operators, giving businesses legal certainty and a more competitive market. It also sets out steps to make space safer and more sustainable: making space objects trackable, reducing space debris, and creating a cybersecurity risk assessment suited to space infrastructure. It would also introduce a common way of measuring the environmental impact of space activities in the EU.

The rules would cover the authorisation, registration and supervision of space activities by providers based in the EU. Providers based outside the EU, as well as international organisations, would also need to register and be supervised when offering space-based data or services in the EU. The proposal further includes orbit traffic management rules, using collision avoidance services, along with provisions on governance and enforcement, a Union Space Label, and capacity-building measures.

posts.title: EU Emissions Trading System: heat and fuel benchmark values for 2026–2030
posts.label: 🤝 Provisional deal between Parliament & Council confirmed
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to amend Directive 2003/87/EC (EU Emissions Trading System – ETS) by revising the heat and fuel benchmark values used for the free allocation of emission allowances for the 2026–2030 period.
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: free allocation to installations in the system for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Union (EU ETS) is determined based on harmonised Union-wide benchmarks reflecting the performance of the most efficient installations. The ex-ante Union-wide benchmarks are established in Annex I to Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/331. The Commission updates the benchmark values for each five-year period for free allocation referred to in Article 11 of Directive 2003/87/EC in accordance with the rules laid down in Article 10a of that Directive.
To address concerns expressed by certain industrial sectors in the context of updating the benchmark values until 2030 and provide additional protection against the risk of carbon leakage, the quantity of allowances to be allocated for free for the period from 2026 to 2030, determined by the heat and fuel benchmarks (‘fallback benchmarks’), should be increased.
CONTENT: therefore, this proposal amends Article 10a of Directive 2003/87/EC regarding the determination of the revised values for the heat and fuel benchmarks until 2030.
The proposal provides for the adjustment to the maximum annual update rate to be applied to heat and fuel benchmarks for the update by the Commission of those benchmark values until 2030. In that case, the adjusted percentage rate value to be applied will reflect the highest possible upwards adjustment to free allocation levels determined by the heat and fuel benchmarks by fully using the available allowances that can be allocated free of charge for 2026 to 2030, amounting to around 80 million allowances , while at the same time not triggering the application of the cross-sectoral correction factor.
The minimum update rate remains unchanged. The reference periods, datasets and overall methodology to update the benchmark values remain unchanged.
The benchmark values will be adjusted for the period from 2027 to 2030. The adjustment to free allocation levels for the year 2026 will be implemented through an update of the benchmark values for the year 2027 applying a maximum update percentage rate value that makes use of 40 % of the additional amount referred to in Article 10a(5a) and ensures that no reduction pursuant to Article 10a(5) applies.
posts.whatsNext: The deal is provisional: it still needs a plenary vote in Parliament and formal adoption by the Council. Although confirmation is expected, either institution can still decline.

aiSummaries.text:
This proposal changes how many free emission allowances EU industries receive under the Emissions Trading System for 2026 to 2030. It amends the EU law that sets out the rules for updating the benchmark values used to decide free allocation, specifically the heat and fuel benchmarks, which are used as a fallback. The change is meant to respond to concerns from some industrial sectors and to give extra protection against carbon leakage, the risk that production moves to places with weaker carbon rules.

The proposal raises the maximum annual rate at which these heat and fuel benchmark values can be adjusted up to 2030. The aim is to give the largest possible increase in free allocation from these benchmarks, using around 80 million allowances that can be given out free for 2026 to 2030. The adjustment is designed so that it does not trigger the cross-sectoral correction factor, which would otherwise reduce allocations across sectors.

The minimum update rate stays the same, and so do the reference periods, data sets and overall method for updating the benchmarks. The adjusted values will apply from 2027 to 2030. The extra allocation for 2026 will be handled through the 2027 update, using a maximum update rate that uses 40% of the additional amount set out in the law and ensures no reduction applies.

The European Parliament will decide on the proposal under the ordinary legislative procedure, on an equal footing with the Council of the EU.

posts.title: European Competitiveness Fund
posts.label: 🧭 Negotiating mandate for trilogue talks
posts.summary:
PURPOSE : to establish a European Competitiveness Fund including a specific programme on defence research and innovation.
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: on 16 July 2025, the European Commission unveiled its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034 , a EUR 2 trillion budget designed to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, competitiveness, and resilience. This new MFF will significantly enhance the EU's capacity to deliver on core policies while addressing new and emerging priorities.
The Union is facing a defining period for its future, from a political, economic, social, environmental, climate and security perspective, including increased risks of conventional military threats. To regain and reinforce its competitive edge, it is essential that the Union revives the innovation cycle by developing its disruptive innovation capacity and investing in emerging, cutting-edge and strategic technologies with significant economic potential. To ensure its autonomy in the global economy, the Union should guarantee its technological and industrial leadership in strategic sectors, starting with critical raw materials supply chains, to develop and manufacture strategic technologies in Europe, as well as mitigate risks affecting its security and resilience emanating from critical external dependencies.
CONTENT: the proposed regulation establishes the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) as part of the multiannual Framework Programme for 2028-2034, including a specific programme on defence research and innovation and lays down the objectives of the ECF.
A new European Competitiveness Fund will invest in strategic technologies, to benefit the entire Single Market. The Fund, operating under one rulebook, and offering a single gateway to funding applicants, will simplify and accelerate EU funding and catalyse private and public investment.
Its general objectives are to:
- establish an investment capacity to support European competitiveness in strategic technologies and sectors, including innovation, decarbonisation, and resilience, through a more seamless investment journey from fundamental research, applied research to deployment and manufacturing;
- leverage the funding tools of the EU Budget to unlock private, institutional and national investment in support of strategic technologies and sectors, including for research and innovation, in the EU.
The proposed financial envelope for the implementation of the ECF for the period from 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2034 will be EUR 234.3 billion . The Fund will focus its support on four policy windows reflecting strategic priorities crucial to Union competitiveness and resilience:
1) A Clean Transition and Industrial Decarbonisation window with a budget of EUR 26.2 billion ;
2) A Health, Biotech, Agriculture and Bioeconomy window with a budget of EUR 20.4 billion ;
3) A Digital Leadership window with a budget of EUR 51.5 billion ;
4) A Resilience and Security, Defence Industry, and Space window with a budget of EUR 125.2 billion .
Its open architecture would help the Fund respond quickly to new challenges and priorities by providing overall direction and strategy. This new architecture would allow for the setting of policy priorities at the level of each window, to effectively target support from applied research to manufacturing and deployment, including infrastructure and specific skills, relying on funding tools adapted to the projects’ needs and derisking investment by offering an appropriate leverage/impact ratio of the Union budget. In addition, the Horizon Europe framework programme for Research and Innovation will be tightly connected to the components of the ECF to ensure a seamless investment journey from idea to market.
The proposal also sets up a legal framework aiming at ensuring security of supply, removing investment obstacles and production bottlenecks and supporting the competitiveness of the Union’s industrial base.
ECF toolbox
The proposal introduces the ‘ECF toolbox’. The ECF will flexibly mobilise the entire financial toolbox provided by the Union budget (including loans, grants, equity, quasi-equity, blending, procurement and guarantees). The budgetary guarantee and financial instruments would become available to all the policy windows, making them usable across areas of funding under a single Fund .
Simplification
The proposal introduces Project Advisory services, supports SME collaboration, and streamlines access to funding. It establishes a centralised Project Advisory for investment support across all policy windows, business support services and a Union business network to bolster SMEs and startups to promote their growth, access to Union funding and investments through advisory and partnering services.

aiSummaries.text:
The European Commission has proposed a European Competitiveness Fund to help the EU invest in strategic technologies and sectors, including a specific programme on defence research and innovation. The European Parliament would decide on the proposal through the ordinary legislative procedure, on an equal footing with the Council. The aim is to strengthen Europe's competitiveness, resilience and autonomy, especially as the Union faces economic, security and climate pressures and wants to keep its technological and industrial leadership in areas such as critical raw materials.

The Fund would operate from 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2034 with a proposed budget of EUR 234.3 billion. It would be organised around four policy windows: a Clean Transition and Industrial Decarbonisation window (EUR 26.2 billion), a Health, Biotech, Agriculture and Bioeconomy window (EUR 20.4 billion), a Digital Leadership window (EUR 51.5 billion), and a Resilience and Security, Defence Industry, and Space window (EUR 125.2 billion).

Its main goals are to support a smoother path for projects from early research through applied research to manufacturing and deployment, and to use EU budget funds to attract private, institutional and national investment into strategic technologies, including research and innovation.

The Fund would work under a single set of rules and give applicants one point of entry. It would be able to use the full range of EU budget tools, such as loans, grants, equity, guarantees and procurement, across all four windows. The Fund's design is meant to let it respond quickly to new priorities.

To make access easier, the proposal creates a centralised advisory service for investment support across all windows, along with business support and a network to help small and medium-sized enterprises and startups grow and find EU funding and investors.

posts.title: Connecting Europe Facility 2028–2034
posts.label: 🧭 Negotiating mandate for trilogue talks
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to establish the Connecting Europe Facility for the period 2028-2034.
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: on 16 July 2025, the European Commission unveiled its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034 , a EUR 2 trillion budget designed to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, competitiveness, and resilience. This new MFF will significantly enhance the EU's capacity to deliver on core policies while addressing new and emerging priorities.
Based on the positive experience from the implementation of the previous Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) programmes, the Commission proposes to continue the implementation of the new programme, for both transport and energy, with direct management by the Commission and an executive agency.
This proposal aims to set the legal basis for CEF for the period 2028-2034.
CONTENT: the proposed regulation establishes the Connecting Europe Facility and lays down the objectives of the Programme, its budget for the period 2028-2034, the forms of Union funding and the rules for providing such funding.
A financial envelope of EUR 81.4 billion is included under this new framework for the Connecting Europe Facility for investments in trans-European networks for transport and energy infrastructure, including military mobility and renewable energy projects.
The distribution of the amount will be as follows:
- EUR 51.5 billion for the specific objectives on transport and military mobility ;
- EUR 29.9 billion for the specific objectives on energy .
General objectives
The general objectives of the programme are to build, develop, secure, modernise and complete the trans-European networks in the transport and energy sectors, facilitate military mobility on the trans-European transport networks, facilitate cross-border cooperation in the field of renewable energy, and facilitate the synergies among the transport and energy sectors.
In the transport sector , CEF contributes to the completion of core network of the trans-European transport network (TEN-T) by 2030 and the extended core network by 2040 through building and upgrading infrastructure that is required for seamless cross-border transport operations. This will lead to a high-performing network for passengers and goods transportation. CEF also supports the adaptation of relevant parts of the TEN-T network to military mobility requirements.
In the field of military mobility , the Programme aims to contribute to enabling transportation of military equipment and personnel across the EU at speed and scale, taking into account the military expertise at EU level.
In the energy sector , CEF contributes to the development of projects of common interest and projects of mutual interest, with a view to promoting the completion of the Energy Union, the integration of an efficient and competitive internal energy market and the interoperability of networks across borders and sectors, to facilitating decarbonisation of the economy, to promoting energy efficiency and to ensuring security of supply.
Furthermore, CEF facilitates cross-border cooperation in the field of renewable energy, through cross-border renewable energy projects or competitive bidding for new renewable energy projects under the Union renewable energy financing mechanism.
The programme should be operational with the start of the next MFF beginning of 2028.

The proposal sits within the next long-term EU budget, a proposed 2 trillion euro framework meant to strengthen Europe's independence, competitiveness and resilience. The program is planned to continue the approach used in earlier Connecting Europe Facility programs, with the Commission managing it directly through an executive agency.

posts.title: Association of the overseas countries and territories with the EU including EU/Greenland/Denmark relations
posts.label: 🗳️ Parliament adopted its opinion (consultation)
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to amend Decision (EU) 2021/1764 to ensure the continuation of the partnership between the Union and the overseas countries and territories (OCTs) under the 2028-2034 multiannual financial framework (MFF).
PROPOSED ACT: Council Decision.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the Council adopts the act after consulting the European Parliament but without being obliged to follow its opinion.
BACKGROUND: this proposal is made in the context of the future multiannual financial framework (MFF) (2028-2034) which has the political ambition of delivering on the Union’s priorities while acting with strength and unity on the global stage over the next decade.
One such priority is stepping up support under the Council Decision on the association of the OCTs with the European Union, including relations between the European Union on one hand, and Greenland and Denmark on the other (Decision on Overseas Association, including Greenland - DOAG), to which the Commission is proposing an amendment.
The 13 OCTs, linked to Denmark, France, and the Netherlands, represent approximately 1 million inhabitants and have the largest EEZ in the world (15 million km²). They are not part of the EU, the single market, or the Schengen area, but their inhabitants are European citizens.
Unlike the NDICI - Global Europe, which establishes a financing instrument (2021-2027), the DOAG is a Council decision that establishes (i) an association of the OCTs with the Union in accordance with the provisions of the Treaty, and (ii) a financing programme for the association. The DOAG does not include a sunset clause linked to the duration of the MFF (with the exception of its financing programme). For this reason, it cannot be merged with Global Europe.
The objectives and mechanisms of the DOAG remain relevant and appropriate. However, given its sunset clause, the financing programme for the association must be resubmitted, including its financial envelope and implementation arrangements.
CONTENT: the proposal seeks to amend Decision (EU) 2021/1764 on the Association of the OCTs with the European Union including relations between the European Union on the one hand, and Greenland and Denmark on the other.
General objective
The general objective of the amending decision is to promote the sustainable economic and social development of the OCTs and to establish close economic relations between them and the Union as a whole.
The association will pursue this general objective by:
- enhancing the OCTs’ competitiveness,
- strengthening the OCTs’ resilience,
- reducing their economic and environmental vulnerability and
- promoting cooperation between them and other partners.
Another aim of this amendment is to preserve the existing ties between the Union on the one hand, and Greenland and Denmark on the other, acknowledging the increased geostrategic position of Greenland in the Arctic, and to preserve existing ties between the Union and the other OCTs, acknowledging their geostrategic positions in the Caribbean, the Indian Ocean, the Atlantic, and the Pacific.
Specific objectives
The specific objectives of this decision are the following:
- to foster and support cooperation with OCTs , including in addressing their major challenges and reaching the sustainable development goals;
- to support and to cooperate with Greenland in addressing its major challenges , notably by raising the education level and strengthening the capacity of its public administration to formulate and implement national policies; and
- to support the sustainable development of strategic sectors - including critical raw materials, renewable energy, secured and trusted digital connectivity, and sustainable tourism - within the framework of a strengthened partnership between the EU and Greenland.
Boosting the strategic investment agenda under the Global Gateway
To bring the EU-OCTs partnership more in line with the commitments under the Global Gateway strategy, it is proposed to merge allocations for territorial (bilateral) and regional cooperation for OCTs, and prepare a separate financing envelope for Greenland, dividing financing between cooperation with the OCTs other than Greenland, and cooperation with Greenland, while providing for flexible implementation modalities.
Reinforcing coherence with the broader EU financing architecture
It is proposed to further reinforce the ‘external’ DOAG dimension specifying the eligibility and access of the OCTs to relevant Union programmes and external financing instruments by consistently applying related cross-references/mirror clauses across all relevant basic acts. The objective is to increase the complementarities of EU actions and strengthen the integration of the OCTs into the EU’s competitiveness agenda.
Strengthening focus and improving the structure of the dialogue with the OCTs
- An ‘OCTs-EU Forum’ will meet every two years to bring together the OCTs’ authorities, representatives of the Member States and the Commission. Members of the European Parliament, representatives of the EIB and representatives of the outermost regions will, where appropriate, be associated with the OCTs-EU Forum.
- Trilateral consultations between the Commission, the OCTs and the Member States to which they are linked will be organised at least three times a year on the initiative of the Commission or at the request of OCTs and of the Member States to which they are linked.
Multiannual indicative programmes, action plans and measures
The Commission will adopt, pursuant to this Decision, multiannual indicative programmes. Programming documents, action plans and measures will be adopted by means of implementing acts, with the exception of action plans and individual measures for which Union financing does not exceed EUR 2 million and special and support measures for which Union financing does not exceed EUR 5 million.
Budgetary implications
The European Commission proposes to allocate an indicative financial envelope of EUR 999 million (in current prices) to the association’s funding programme for 2028-2034.

The Council would adopt the measure after consulting the European Parliament, but would not have to follow Parliament's opinion.

The reason for the change is that the current decision has a sunset clause tied to the budget period, so its funding programme has to be submitted again, including its financial amount and how it will be carried out. The 13 OCTs, linked to Denmark, France and the Netherlands, have about 1 million inhabitants and the largest exclusive economic zone in the world. They are not part of the EU, the single market or the Schengen area, but their inhabitants are European citizens. The decision also covers relations with Greenland and Denmark, reflecting Greenland's growing strategic importance in the Arctic.

The overall aim is to promote sustainable economic and social development in the OCTs and to build close economic ties between them and the EU. The partnership would work toward this by improving the OCTs' competitiveness and resilience, reducing their economic and environmental vulnerability, and encouraging cooperation with other partners. It also has specific goals: supporting cooperation with the OCTs on their major challenges and the UN sustainable development goals, helping Greenland raise education levels and strengthen its public administration, and supporting sustainable development in strategic sectors such as critical raw materials, renewable energy, secure digital connectivity and sustainable tourism.

Several changes are proposed to make the partnership work better. Territorial and regional funding for the OCTs would be combined, with a separate funding share for Greenland, and implementation would allow flexibility. posts.title: Union Civil Protection Mechanism and Union support for health emergency preparedness and response
posts.label: ↩️ Plenary sent the file back to committee
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to provide for the Union Civil Protection Mechanism for the period 2028-2034.
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: on 16 July 2025, the Commission unveiled its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034 (MFF), a budget of almost EUR 2 trillion between 2028 and 2034 designed to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, competitiveness, and resilience. This proposal is part of a set of sectoral regulations governing programmes under the next MFF.
Given the significant increase in the number and severity of natural and human-induced hazards in recent years, enhanced cooperation in the field of civil protection at Union level is necessary to create a resilient Union with the necessary capacities to anticipate and manage such risks and threats, whatever their nature of origin. The Union Civil Protection Mechanism should fulfil this role by strengthening cooperation and coordination between Member States in order to improve the overall capacity to prevent, prepare for and respond to them.
CONTENT: the proposed regulation provides for the Union Civil Protection Mechanism and sets out Union support for health emergency preparedness and response. It defines the objectives, the budget for the period 2028-2034, the forms of Union financing, and the rules for granting that financing.
General objective
The proposed regulation aims to ensure the protection of people, the environment and property, as well as cultural heritage, against all types of natural and human-induced disasters, including serious cross-border threats to health. It will allow for cross-sectoral coordination in situations where other EU crisis response or risk management mechanisms are applied.
The indicative financial envelope for the implementation of the regulation for the period 2028-2034 is set at EUR 10 675 000 000 in current prices.
The specific objectives pursued are as follows:
- strengthen understanding and anticipation of disaster risks and threats , including those related to climate change and public health, and work proactively to prevent or mitigate their potential impacts, foster prevention and preparedness, and enhance collaboration between civil protection, health and other relevant authorities;
- facilitate capacity building at Union and Member State level, including by encouraging and increasing the uptake and use of research and innovation results in disaster and crisis response, by providing and implementing capacity building programmes such as training and exercises, peer reviews and deployment of experts;
- strengthen preparedness at Member State and Union level, including at all levels of society by: (i) supporting the development of early warning systems to detect and communicate imminent threats of disasters, (ii) promoting the integration of disaster risk reduction and preparedness considerations into policies and financial frameworks at national and Union level, (iii) facilitating preparedness and resilience of all actors and stakeholders, including all levels of government, civil and military authorities, civil society and the private sector;
- facilitate a rapid and effective response within the Union as well as outside the Union, following a request for assistance;
- support the preparedness and response of Member States and the Union to cross-sectoral crises;
- strengthen capacities for prevention, preparedness and rapid response to serious cross-border threats to health and improve the supply of medical countermeasures.
The Commission should work with the High Representative to help develop measures to improve civil-military preparedness and response coordination within the Union, in consultation with Member States.
Emergency Response Coordination Centre
Coordination efforts will be strengthened and further refined through the capacity building of the Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCC) and the establishment of a dedicated Crisis Coordination Hub to help Member States anticipate and manage the consequences of crises across all sectors.
The co-financing rates and operational rules established in Decision No 1313/2013 and under the EU4Health programme will be simplified to allow for more efficient and flexible implementation in the event of a fast-evolving crisis.

aiSummaries.text:
The proposed regulation would set up the Union Civil Protection Mechanism for 2028 to 2034, along with EU support for preparing for and responding to health emergencies. Its aim is to protect people, the environment, property and cultural heritage from all kinds of natural and human-caused disasters, including serious cross-border health threats. The European Parliament would decide on it through the ordinary legislative procedure, on an equal footing with the Council.

The background is a sharp rise in the number and severity of hazards in recent years. The proposal argues that stronger cooperation and coordination between Member States is needed so the EU can better prevent, prepare for and respond to these risks, whatever their origin. It is part of a wider set of rules for programmes under the next long-term EU budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028 to 2034, which the Commission put forward in July 2025 as a budget of almost EUR 2 trillion.

The regulation's specific goals include understanding and anticipating disaster risks, including those linked to climate change and public health, and acting early to reduce their impact. They also include building skills through training, exercises, peer reviews and expert deployments, and strengthening preparedness at every level of society, such as early warning systems and better links between civil protection, health and other authorities. Further goals are responding quickly and effectively both inside and outside the EU when assistance is requested, supporting responses to crises that span several sectors, and improving prevention and response to serious cross-border health threats, including the supply of medical countermeasures.

The indicative budget for 2028 to 2034 is EUR 10,675,000,000 in current prices. The Commission would also work with the High Representative, consulting Member States, to improve coordination between civil and military preparedness and response.

To support this, the Emergency Response Coordination Centre would be strengthened and a dedicated Crisis Coordination Hub would be created to help Member States anticipate and manage crises across all sectors. The rules on co-financing rates and operations would also be simplified so that funding and action can move faster and more flexibly during fast-changing crises.

posts.title: Geographical indications: aligning EU rules with changes to the provisions under the Lisbon Agreement
posts.label: 🗳️ Parliament adopted its 1st-reading position
posts.whatsNext: Council formal adoption is next, often without debate.
posts.summary:
The European Parliament adopted by 613 votes to 3, with 0 abstentions, a legislative resolution on the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Regulation (EU) 2019/1753 as regards amendments adopted by the Assembly of the Lisbon Union on 14 July 2025 to the Common Regulations under the Lisbon Agreement on Appellations of Origin and Geographical Indications.
The text recalled that on 14 July 2025, during the 66th Series of Meetings of the Assemblies of the Member States of the World Intellectual Property Organization, the Assembly of the Lisbon Union adopted amendments to the Common Regulations under the Lisbon Agreement for the Protection of Appellations of Origin and their International Registration and the Geneva Act of the Lisbon Agreement on Appellations of Origin and Geographical Indications. Those new rules entered into force on 1 July 2026.
As a consequence of the adoption of those amendments to the Common Regulations, Regulation (EU) 2019/1753 should be amended to enable the Union to continue to meet its obligations as a Contracting Party to the Geneva Act and to make use of the new procedural options provided for in the amended Common Regulations.
The European Parliament adopted its position at first reading by amending the Commission's proposal as follows:
Geographical indications
For the purposes of this Regulation, the term “geographical indications” covers:
(a) appellations of origin and geographical indications within the meaning of the Geneva Act;
(b) protected designations of origin and protected geographical indications for wine and agricultural products, as well as geographical indications for spirit drinks, within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 of the European Parliament and of the Council; and
(c) protected geographical indications for craft and industrial products within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2023/2411 of the European Parliament and of the Council.
In respect of appellations of origin relating to craft and industrial products which are the subject of an international registration, protection in the Union should be construed as specified in Regulation (EU) 2023/2411.
Modifications of Union’s and Member States’ registrations of geographical indications in the International Register
The text provides that following the approval of an amendment of the product specification concerning the name or classification of the product that implies a modification of the type of good or goods under the Geneva Act of geographical indications originating in the Union and protected, the Commission or the Office, should present to the International Bureau a request for entry of a modification of the name or of the type of good or goods in relation to the corresponding geographical indication registered in the International Register.
The Commission or, as applicable, the Office, should be exempt from the obligation to request the entry in the International Register of a modification in cases where the Member State in which the geographical indication originates, by the date on which the amendment of the product specification of the geographical indication has been approved in accordance with Union law, requests the Commission or, as applicable, the Office, to cancel the corresponding registration in the International Register.
Furthermore, at the request of a Member State, the Commission or the Office may request the updating of information relating to the geographical area, quality, reputation or characteristics of the product.
Modifications and corrections in relation to third country geographical indications registered in the International Register
The amended text extends the European procedures applicable to a modification of the name or of the type of good or goods in relation to geographical indications registered in the International Register. Upon the request of a Member State or upon its own initiative, the Commission or, in respect of geographical indications for craft and industrial products, the Office, may apply these procedures to a modification of the particulars concerning the quality, reputation or characteristics of products or to a correction in relation to a geographical indication registered in the International Register.
Entry into force
In order to allow for right holders in the Union to benefit as soon as possible from the ability to request the entry in the International Register of modifications of registrations under the Geneva Act, as well as to enable the Union, as soon as possible, to refuse protection under the Geneva Act following a modification or correction by another Contracting Party to the Geneva Act, this Regulation should enter into force on the day following that of its publication.

aiSummaries.text:
The European Parliament has approved a change to an EU regulation so that the EU can keep following the international rules on protected place names, such as Champagne or Parmigiano-Reggiano, under the Geneva Act of the Lisbon Agreement. The change follows amendments adopted in July 2025 by the Lisbon Union, which take effect on 1 July 2026. The vote was 613 in favour, 3 against and no abstentions.

The new rules cover three kinds of protected names: appellations of origin and geographical indications under the Geneva Act; protected designations of origin and geographical indications for wine, agricultural products and spirit drinks; and protected geographical indications for craft and industrial products. For craft and industrial products that are internationally registered, protection in the EU follows the rules in the separate regulation that governs them.

If an EU product's specification is changed in a way that alters its name or the type of goods it covers, the European Commission or the relevant EU Office must ask the international register to record that change. This is not required if the Member State where the product comes from asks, before the change is approved, for the international registration to be cancelled. At a Member State's request, the Commission or the Office can also ask for updates to information about the geographical area, quality, reputation or characteristics of a product.

The EU can also apply these same procedures to changes or corrections affecting names from non-EU countries that are registered internationally. This can happen at a Member State's request or on the EU's own initiative, and can cover changes to the quality, reputation or characteristics of a product, not just its name or type.

The regulation will take effect the day after it is published. This is so EU right holders can request changes to their international registrations as soon as possible, and so the EU can quickly refuse protection when another country changes or corrects a registration under the Geneva Act.

posts.title: European Chemicals Agency and amending regulations
posts.label: 🗳️ Parliament adopted its 1st-reading position
posts.whatsNext: Council formal adoption is next, often without debate.
posts.summary:
The European Parliament adopted by 561 votes to 13, with 39 abstentions, a legislative on the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the European Chemicals Agency and amending Regulations (EC) No 1907/2006, (EU) No 528/2012, (EU) No 649/2012 and (EU) 2019/1021.
The European Parliament adopted its position at first reading by amending the Commission's proposal as follows:
Objectives and tasks of the Agency
The Agency should: (i) contribute to the implementation and enforcement of relevant Union legislation and policies related to the hazards, risks, safe use and environmental sustainability of chemicals; (ii) provide scientific opinions and advice and independent information on all those matters, monitor emerging chemical risks and collect or generate data on chemicals, and communicate on those matters.
In the fulfilment of its objectives, the Agency aims to:
- contribute to a high level of protection of human health and the environment , including the protection of vulnerable groups, and shall aim to contribute to the free circulation of substances in the internal market;
- deliver a high level of quality, coherence and consistency in the assessment and management of chemicals across the Union, while enhancing competitiveness and innovation, taking into account the specific needs of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
The Agency should also promote and strengthen expertise regarding the substitution of hazardous chemicals as well as regarding the development and use of non-animal approaches and emerging methodologies.
In addition, the Agency should, inter alia: (i) ensure that conflicts of interest are prevented or managed in order to guarantee the Agency's independence and credibility with stakeholders and the general public; (ii) organise annual training for staff and committee members and share knowledge with all stakeholders.
Composition of the Management Board and Committees
The Management Board should be composed of: (a) one representative from each Member State, nominated by that Member State and appointed by the Council; (b) six persons appointed by the Commission, namely, three representatives of the Commission and three persons representing interested parties; (c) two independent persons appointed by the European Parliament in the performance of their duties.
In addition to the tasks referred to in the regulation, the Committees , at the request of the Executive Director, should provide technical and scientific support to measures aimed at improving cooperation among the Union, Member States, international organisations and third countries on scientific and technical issues relating to the safety of substances as well as active participation in technical assistance and capacity building activities on the sound management of chemicals in developing countries.
Budget and fees
Within the limits of the Agency’s budget adopted in accordance with Union budgetary rules, the Agency should determine the internal allocation of financial resources across its activities and tasks, in line with its mandate and programming documents. The Agency should report to the European Parliament and to the Council annually, as part of its consolidated annual activity report, on the reserve’s opening balance, inflows, outflows, and justifications.
By two years from the date of application of this Regulation, and every five years thereafter, the Commission should submit an assessment of the functioning of the reserve to the European Parliament and to the Council. Moreover, by two years from the date of application of this Regulation and every five years thereafter, the Commission should evaluate the budgetary adequacy and adapt accordingly the fees payable to the Agency.
Research and innovation
The Agency should assist Member States and the Commission with research and innovation within the fields of competence of the Agency. This assistance will include:
- the promotion of substitution of hazardous chemicals by safer and more sustainable alternative substances and technologies;
- support for the development of regulatory scientific methodologies which include non‑animal approaches for chemicals testing;
- participation in relevant research, development, and innovation activities.
Scientific advice for the European Parliament and Member States
The European Parliament or a Member State should, after having consulted the Commission and considered the comments received from the Commission, submit a request to the Agency to issue scientific advice on matters falling within its competences.
The Agency may refuse a request if it is redundant, falls outside its remit, compromises its missions, or is based on insufficient information. It must publish the reasons for refusal on its website. The Agency will set a response deadline after consulting the parties concerned, with the possibility of a justified extension.
Cooperation
The Agency should also cooperate with other EU bodies, including the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the European Environment Agency (EEA), the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), the European Medicines Agency (EMA), the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) and the European Union Reference Laboratory for alternatives to animal testing (EURL ECVAM) to share advice, data and scientific methods, develop approaches to assessing chemicals without animal testing and promote the 'One Health' approach.
