This proposal would change the EU's existing rules on carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from new cars and light commercial vans, while keeping its climate goals in place. It gives carmakers more flexibility in how they meet those targets, and it updates and simplifies the rules on vehicle labels. The proposal amends Regulation (EU) 2019/631, which has applied since 1 January 2020, and it repeals Directive 1999/94/EC, which is considered outdated. The European Parliament would decide on the proposal under the ordinary legislative procedure, on an equal footing with the Council.

The main change is to the reduction targets. For vans, the 2030 target would drop from a 50% cut to a 40% cut compared with the 2021 baseline. For cars and vans together, the 2035 target would drop from a 100% cut to a 90% cut.

To help meet these targets, the proposal introduces several flexibilities. Before 2035, carmakers could earn extra "super credits" for small, affordable electric cars made in the EU. From 2035, the remaining 10% of emissions could be offset using low-carbon steel made in the Union, or with e-fuels and biofuels.

The proposal also clarifies that all zero-emission N-category vehicles (including N1 and N2) whose mass without the battery is below 2,840 kg count when checking compliance with the CO2 targets.

Finally, the proposal extends vehicle labelling requirements to manufacturers, dealers, and anyone else selling vehicles in the course of a business. Private individuals who only occasionally sell a second-hand car would not be covered. The labelling rules would be placed within Regulation (EU) 2019/631 so they are applied the same way across the Union.

posts.title: Speeding-up environmental assessments (Omnibus VIII on environmental legislation)
posts.label: 🗳️ Lead committee adopted its report
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to accelerate and streamline environmental assessments across the EU.
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: the Union has committed to the accelerated decarbonisation of its economy to achieve climate neutrality, namely net-zero emissions or emissions after the deduction of removals, by 2050.
The findings of the 2024 Draghi report indicate that lengthy and uncertain permit granting procedures are an obstacle for the roll-out of critical projects such as new power supply and grids. The Clean Industrial Deal Communication indicates that it is to speed up permit granting procedures, in particular for the deployment of grids, energy storage and renewables projects, industrial access to energy and industrial decarbonisation projects as well as manufacturing of clean technologies.
Faster permit granting procedures are necessary, amongst other:
- for Data centre projects, EuroHPC supercomputer facilities, AI factories, AI Gigafactories, semiconductor projects;
- for projects supporting the digital transition, for those related to the decarbonisation of maritime and inland ports, airports and railways of trans-European transport network;
- for projects which are critical to ensure food security in the Union.
Furthermore, access to affordable housing is strategic for the European Union’s competitiveness, including for labour mobility.
Procedures linked to environmental assessments should be accelerated and streamlined for plans, programmes and projects across all sectors of the economy by establishing a common acceleration framework for environmental assessments in order to boost EU’s roll out of key technologies, reduce dependencies and strengthen competitiveness. The proposed Regulation provides for such framework, while maintaining the same level of protection of human health and of the environment.
CONTENT: this proposal contains concrete measures to accelerate environmental assessments across the European Union , given their central role in the planning and permitting process. It builds on the existing environmental acquis and provides a common procedural framework for environmental assessments, ensuring that all environmental assessments within the overall permitting process are faster, more efficient, and more cost-effective.
The main elements of the proposal are as follows:
Environmental single point of contact
By 6 months after the entry into force of this Regulation, Member States should establish or designate environmental single points of contact at the relevant administrative level for environmental assessments. Each single point of contact should be responsible for facilitating and coordinating all aspects of the environmental assessments under this Regulation, including for providing information on when an application is considered to be completed.
The single points of contact should adequately staffed and resourced.
Streamlining of environmental assessment procedures
The proposal ensures that in the case of plans, programmes, or projects for which there is an obligation to carry out assessments of the effects on the environment or a screening arising simultaneously from Directive 2001/42/EC, Directive 2011/92/EU, Council Directive 92/43/EEC, Directive 2009/147/EC and Directive 2000/60/EC. Member States apply coordinated or joint procedures fulfilling all the requirements of those Union legislative acts.
Changes to projects
Changes or extensions of projects, such as repurposing of pipelines or of industrial sites, and extension of their operation period and modifications to ensure decarbonisation, shall only be subject to screening by the competent authorities in order to determine if they are likely to have significant effects on the environment. Those changes or extensions shall be subject to an environmental assessment only where they involve major works that represent risks that are similar to or greater than, in terms of their effects on the environment, to those posed by the original project.
Duration of due diligence and environmental assessments
The proposal sets out maximum time limits for impact assessments under the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive and the Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) Directive, in order to respond to the widespread demand to accelerate environmental assessments.
Protected species
This provision outlines that occasional harm to protected bird and other species during project activities is not considered deliberate be considered to be deliberate within the meaning of Directive 2009/147/EC and Directive 92/43/EEC if appropriate and proportionate mitigation measures are used and best technologies are considered, requiring Member States to monitor effectiveness and adapt measures to prevent significant impacts on species populations.
Furthermore, the proposal:
- requires effective collaboration among national authorities in assessing transboundary environmental effects for plans requiring multi-state decisions, with the Commission available as a facilitator for joint procedures;
- aims to fully digitise impact assessments procedures and related data management. In the interim, project developers should be allowed to submit their applications digitally;
- encourages Member States to bear the administrative costs (levies) associated with the environmental assessments for a given project, in order to reduce costs for project developers across the covered priority projects.
posts.whatsNext: A negotiating mandate for talks with the Council would usually follow, or the report goes straight to a plenary vote. No deadline applies.

aiSummaries.text:
The European Union is proposing a regulation to speed up and simplify the environmental assessments that projects and plans must go through before they can be approved, without lowering the level of protection for human health and the environment. The aim is to help the EU build key technologies, reduce its reliance on outside sources, and stay competitive, while working toward climate neutrality by 2050. The proposal notes that slow and uncertain permit procedures currently hold back important projects such as power supply and grid expansion, data centres, supercomputer and AI facilities, semiconductor plants, transport and port upgrades, and projects that help secure food supplies. It also says that affordable housing matters for the EU's competitiveness and labour mobility.

The main measures are as follows. Each Member State must set up or designate, within 6 months of the regulation entering into force, an environmental single point of contact at the relevant administrative level. These contact points are to coordinate all parts of the environmental assessments and tell applicants when their application is considered complete, and they should be properly staffed and resourced. Where several environmental assessments apply to the same plan, programme or project under the listed EU directives, Member States must run them through coordinated or joint procedures that still meet all the requirements of those directives.

Changes to existing projects, such as repurposing pipelines or industrial sites, extending operating periods, or making changes to support decarbonisation, will only need a screening by authorities to judge whether they are likely to have significant environmental effects. A full environmental assessment is required only if those changes involve major works carrying risks similar to or greater than those of the original project. The proposal also sets maximum time limits for impact assessments under the Environmental Impact Assessment and Strategic Environmental Assessment directives.

On protected species, occasional harm to protected birds and other species during project work will not be treated as deliberate harm if suitable and proportionate mitigation measures are used and the best available technologies are considered. Member States must monitor how well these measures work and adjust them to prevent significant effects on species populations.

Finally, the proposal requires national authorities to cooperate effectively on environmental effects that cross borders, with the Commission able to help run joint procedures. It aims to fully digitise assessment procedures and data management, and in the meantime lets project developers submit applications digitally. It also encourages Member States to cover the administrative charges for environmental assessments of priority projects, to lower costs for developers.

posts.title: Market stability reserve for the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS): ceasing the invalidation of allowances
posts.label: 🤝 Lead committee approved the trilogue deal
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to amend the EU greenhouse gas emission trading system (ETS's) Market Stability Reserve (MSR) with a view to enhancing stability and predictability.
PROPOSED ACT: Council Decision.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: Directive (EU) 2018/410 amended Decision (EU) 2015/1814 concerning the operation of the market stability reserve (MSR) for the Union greenhouse gas emission trading system (EU ETS). The purpose was to improve the effectiveness and stability of the EU ETS in the long term, including by invalidating from 2023 onwards allowances, in the reserve above a threshold equal to the total number of allowances auctioned during the previous year. This threshold was changed by Directive (EU) 2023/959 from a dynamic threshold to a fixed threshold of 400 million allowances from 2024, to ensure that the level of allowances in the reserve is predictable.
Since the provision for the invalidation of allowances in the reserve entered into force, a total of 3.2 billion allowances have been invalidated and the balance between supply and demand has been restored to the EU ETS.
Allowing a greater number of allowances to remain in the MSR rather than invalidating them could provide an essential liquidity buffer to manage future market tightness after the mid-2030s and beyond. For this reason, allowances in the reserve should no longer be invalidated to allow a larger number of allowances to remain in the reserve. This will increase the firepower of the MSR for possible future releases in the next decade to balance the market.
CONTENT: this proposal therefore provides for a targeted amendment to Decision (EU) 2015/1814 on the market stability reserve under the EU Emissions Trading System to discontinue invalidation , without changing the overall design of the MSR. The purpose is to improve its ability to ensure future market stability and resilience based on up-to-date information by allowing a greater number of allowances to remain in the reserve as a liquidity and stability buffer.
More specifically, it sets an end date for the provision in the MSR Decision which invalidates EU ETS allowances above a level of 400 million. It should cease to apply from the date of entry into force of this amendment. The earlier the proposal is adopted, the more allowances could be prevented from being invalidated and could be held in the MSR.
Monitoring
The upcoming review of the MSR will, based on an in-depth forward-looking analysis, assess the appropriateness of the parameters used to determine whether intakes or releases take place and propose changes where necessary to enable the MSR to continue to effectively address both surplus and scarcity situations, to achieve EU climate targets.
posts.whatsNext: The deal is provisional: it still needs a plenary vote in Parliament and formal adoption by the Council. Although confirmation is expected, either institution can still decline.

aiSummaries.text:
The EU is proposing a change to its carbon market's Market Stability Reserve, a buffer that holds spare emission allowances. The change would stop the reserve from permanently cancelling allowances above a set level of 400 million. Instead, a larger number of allowances would stay in the reserve.

The reason is that cancelling allowances has already restored the balance between supply and demand in the EU carbon market, with 3.2 billion allowances invalidated so far. Keeping more allowances in the reserve would give it a bigger cushion to release into the market if it becomes tight after the mid-2030s and beyond.

The proposal is a narrow change. It sets an end date for the cancellation rule, which would stop applying once the amendment takes effect, and it leaves the overall design of the reserve as it is. The sooner the change is adopted, the more allowances could be kept in the reserve rather than cancelled.

The upcoming review of the reserve will look at whether the rules that decide when allowances are added to or released from it still work well. It may propose changes so the reserve can handle both surplus and shortage and help the EU meet its climate targets.

posts.title: Combating the sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child sexual abuse material. Recast
posts.label: 🤝 Lead committee approved the trilogue deal
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to revise the current directive on child sexual abuse and sexual exploitation.
PROPOSED ACT: Directive of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: in 2020, the Commission presented an EU Strategy for a more effective fight against child sexual abuse. This Strategy set out eight initiatives aiming to ensure full implementation and, where needed, further development of the legal framework to combat child sexual abuse and exploitation.
The Strategy recognised the need to assess whether the current EU criminal law framework, namely Directive 2011/93/EU on combating the sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, is fit for purpose considering the societal and technological changes over the past decade.
In 2022, the Commission conducted an evaluation to assess the implementation of the Directive, assessing possible legislative gaps, best practices and priority actions at EU level. The study raised concerns related to the exponential growth of online sharing of child sexual abuse material and to the increased possibilities for perpetrators to hide their identity (and conceal their illegal activities), most notably online, thereby escaping investigation and prosecution.
The Commission concluded that a renewed legislative framework is needed at EU level to address the latest developments and to strengthen the prevention and protection of victims.
CONTENT: the proposed directive improves the clarity of the legal landscape for fighting child sexual abuse across Member States.
Overall, the targeted amendments to the Directive are aimed at improving Member State capacity to fight the crime efficiently, in relation to threats and trends that have emerged and evolved in recent years and with new technological developments . New rules applicable to Member States are expected to improve cross-border cooperation , both in terms of investigations and prosecutions , and for victim assistance and support .
The main aspects of the proposal are as follows:
Expanding the definition of criminal offences related to child sexual abuse across Member States : these new offences include livestreaming of child sexual abuse and the possession and exchange of paedophile handbooks. The new rules also update the definitions of the crime to include child sexual abuse material in deep fakes or AI-generated material.
Strengthening prosecution, prevention and support : underreporting of child sexual abuse still constitutes a major challenge in the efforts to stop child sexual abuse and prevent further sexual abuse from taking place. The proposal will set a longer time period during which victims can report the sexual abuse they suffered and seek action against the offender. The new rules will also grant victims a right to financial compensation , to address the long-term harms that child sexual abuse causes. In addition, Member States are required to put in place a coordination mechanism to make best use of available programmes on prevention and assistance to victims.
Stepping up prevention : Member States are also asked to step up investment in awareness raising especially for online risks to ensure that the internet is safer and better for children and young people.
In addition, new requirements will ensure recruiters for activities involving close contact with children and for organisations working against child sexual abuse must request the criminal records of the candidates.
There will also be mandatory reporting of an offence at least by professionals working in close contact with children to address a major challenge in the efforts to stop child sexual abuse.
posts.whatsNext: The deal is provisional: it still needs a plenary vote in Parliament and formal adoption by the Council. Although confirmation is expected, either institution can still decline.

aiSummaries.text:
This proposal would update the existing EU rules on child sexual abuse and exploitation, which date from 2011, so they better match today's threats, especially those happening online. The aim is to help Member States fight these crimes more effectively and to make cooperation across borders on investigations, prosecutions and victim support work better. The European Parliament and the Council would decide on it together, on an equal footing.

The changes come from a 2020 EU strategy and a 2022 review of how the current rules were working. That review raised concern about the rapid growth in online sharing of child sexual abuse material and about how easily offenders can hide their identities and avoid being caught. The Commission concluded that a renewed framework was needed.

The proposal widens the list of crimes covered. New offences would include livestreaming child sexual abuse and possessing or exchanging manuals that encourage paedophilia. The definition would also cover abuse material made with deepfakes or generated by artificial intelligence.

To help victims, the proposal would give them a longer period in which to report the abuse and seek action against the offender. Victims would also gain a right to financial compensation for the long-term harm abuse causes. Member States would have to set up a way to coordinate the prevention and victim assistance programmes already available.

On prevention, Member States would be asked to invest more in awareness campaigns, particularly about online risks, to make the internet safer for children and young people. Recruiters for jobs or activities involving close contact with children, and organisations working against child sexual abuse, would have to request candidates' criminal records. Professionals who work in close contact with children would also be required to report an offence.

posts.title: Programme for agile and rapid defence innovation (AGILE)
posts.label: 📜 Published in the Official Journal
posts.summary:
The European Parliament adopted by 536 votes to 101, with 16 abstentions, a legislative resolution on the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing the Programme for agile and rapid defence innovation (AGILE).
The European Parliament adopted its position at first reading by amending the Commission's proposal as follows:
Programme objectives
The proposed regulation establishes the programme for agile and rapid defence innovation for the period from 1 January 2027 to 31 December 2027.
In addition to the support provided through existing EU instruments, a new programme should be established to provide rapid, agile and targeted support to SMEs to develop innovative defence solutions and ensure their rapid delivery to Member States and associated third countries, with a focus on cost-efficiency in order to meet the challenges faced by the armed forces of Member States and associated third countries, in particular those arising from the war of aggression waged by Russia against Ukraine.
The programme will thereby foster the competitiveness of the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base (EDTIB) and contribute to strengthening the Union’s defence industrial readiness, while reducing strategic dependencies on non-associated third countries across the full spectrum of defence technologies.
The programme should:
- focus on supporting the rapid development of emerging and disruptive defence products and technologies ;
- address the most urgent capability development needs of Member States and associated third countries, taking into consideration the capability priorities identified in the context of the common foreign and security policy (CFSP) and the priority capability areas identified at Union level, as well as NATO standards and other relevant standards, with a particular focus on low-cost defence solutions.
- accelerate the innovation cycles of emerging and disruptive defence products , aligning their development with the urgent needs of Member States and associated third countries, while leveraging the innovation potential of the Union’s defence industry as a whole;
- foster the uptake of such products by Member States , associated third countries and prime contractors, supporting the scaling-up of SME-developed solutions across Europe and their integration into cross-border defence supply chains and strengthening security of supply for defence products within the Union.
Budget
The indicative financial envelope for the implementation of the programme, between 1 January 2027 and 31 December 2027, is EUR 115 million in current prices.
Eligible actions
Actions eligible for funding under the programme may take one or more of the following forms:
- support for the rapid development of emerging and disruptive defence products and, where appropriate, components necessary for their production;
- support for market uptake of emerging and disruptive defence products, including through support for the aggregation of demand and dedicated and iterative field testing and demonstrations with the involvement and feedback of end-users;
- support for the relocation of the establishment of an entity or of its executive management structure to the Union or to an associated third country for the effective implementation of actions, where an entity was previously established or its executive management structure was located in a non-associated third country;
- support for investment readiness, as well as activities to build and strengthen ecosystems, including support for cooperation between SMEs and European defence industrial prime contractors, system integrators and first-tier subcontractors.
The following actions will not be eligible for Union funding: (a) actions for the development of lethal autonomous weapons without the possibility for meaningful human control over selection and engagement decisions when carrying out strikes against humans; (b) actions related to cluster munitions.
Furthermore, actions supported by the programme should not contravene the security and defence interests of the Union and its Member States.
The programme will provide a fast-track, four-month time-to-grant , reinforcing AGILE's role as a nimble complement to the EU's existing defence industrial toolbox.
Sovereignty Seal
Regulation (EU) 2024/795 establishing the Strategic Technologies for Europe (STEP) platform provides for the awarding of a sovereignty seal to projects that meet the minimum quality requirements set out in the programmes listed in that regulation. The Commission should award a sovereignty seal to any project contributing to the achievement of one of the STEP objectives, provided that the project has been assessed and meets the minimum quality requirements provided for in a call for proposals under the regulation concerning the establishment of the AGILE programme.
Monitoring and reporting
The Commission should regularly inform the European Parliament and the Council about the implementation of the programme. By 1 July 2028, the Commission should draw up a report evaluating the impact and effectiveness of the actions supported by the programme. That report should include information on, in particular, the level of participation of SMEs; the geographical distribution of supported entities and the thematic distribution of supported activities.

The European Parliament has approved a plan called AGILE, a programme to quickly support small and medium-sized companies in developing new defence products and getting them to governments and armed forces. The programme runs for 2027 only and has an indicative budget of EUR 115 million. It is meant to add to existing EU defence tools, with a focus on cheaper, fast-to-develop solutions for the needs of EU countries and associated non-EU countries, including those raised by Russia's war against Ukraine. The aim is to strengthen Europe's defence industry, make it more ready to supply itself, and reduce reliance on non-associated third countries.

Funding can cover the rapid development of new defence products and the parts needed to make them, help these products get taken up by buyers through shared demand and hands-on field testing, and support companies that move into the EU or an associated country to carry out projects. The programme promises a fast process, with a four-month time to grant funding. Projects that meet the minimum quality requirements can receive a "sovereignty seal" under the existing STEP regulation. The Commission must keep Parliament and the Council informed about progress and, by 1 July 2028, publish a report on the programme's impact and effectiveness, including how much small companies took part, where supported organisations are located, and which kinds of activities were funded.

posts.title: Exemption of certain N2 electric vehicles from the requirement to install and use a speed limitation device (Omnibus IX on automotive)
posts.label: 🗳️ Lead committee adopted its report
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to amend Directive 92/6/EEC by introducing a targeted exemption for certain N2 category electric vehicles from the obligation to install and use a speed limitation device.
PROPOSED ACT: Directive of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: Article 3(1) of Council Directive 92/6/EEC on the installation and use of speed limitation devices for certain categories of vehicles requires the installation and use of speed limitation devices in vehicles of the category N2 and N3. Under that Article, such vehicles can be used on the road only if equipped with a speed limitation device. The installation requirement has been integrated into motor vehicle type-approval legislation with Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 of the European Parliament and of the Council.
Due to the weight of the battery, battery-electric light commercial vehicles might exceed a weight of 3,5 tonnes and are subject to the requirement to be equipped with speed limitation devices although they have the same payload and use case as light commercial vehicles with an internal combustion engine that are outside the scope of the Regulation (EU) 2019/2144. That requirement imposes unnecessary costs on vehicle manufacturers and enterprises purchasing such vehicles, slowing down the increase in the number of zero-emission light commercial vehicles. It is therefore appropriate to amend Directive 92/6/EEC accordingly with a view to exempting zero-emission vehicles of category N2 with maximum technically permissible laden mass between 3,5 and 4,25 tonnes from the requirement to be equipped with speed limitation devices.
Moreover, Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 is amended in parallel to exempt vehicles of category N2 propelled by means of electricity, with a maximum technically permissible laden mass between 3,5 and 4,25 tonnes, from the requirement to be equipped with speed limitation devices in accordance with UN Regulation No 89.
This proposal forms part of the Automotive Omnibus which aims to remove regulatory barriers that disproportionately affect electric vehicles, in particular in the light commercial and small passenger car segments. It is implemented through two parallel legislative proposals: this proposed Directive and a proposed Regulation .
CONTENT: therefore, the proposed Directive:
- amends Directive 92/6/EEC by introducing a targeted exemption for certain N2 category electric vehicles from the obligation to install and use a speed limitation device. The amendment reflects the specific technical characteristics and operational use of electric N2 vehicles, particularly in urban and short-distance transport. The objective is to remove disproportionate regulatory requirements , support the uptake of zero-emission heavy-duty vehicles , and ensure that speed limitation rules remain appropriate and effective . The exemption aims to facilitate the deployment of electric N2 vehicles while maintaining road safety and coherence with EU transport and climate policies.
posts.whatsNext: A negotiating mandate for talks with the Council would usually follow, or the report goes straight to a plenary vote. No deadline applies.

aiSummaries.text:
This proposal would change EU rules so that certain electric delivery-type trucks do not have to be fitted with a speed limiting device. It amends an existing EU directive, Directive 92/6/EEC, which requires speed limiters on certain goods vehicles, by adding an exemption for electric vehicles in the N2 category.

The exemption covers zero-emission N2 vehicles whose maximum technically permissible laden mass is between 3.5 and 4.25 tonnes. The reason is that battery weight can push some electric light commercial vehicles above 3.5 tonnes, which then brings them under the speed limiter requirement. Comparable petrol or diesel vehicles with the same payload and use do not face that requirement, so the rule adds costs for manufacturers and buyers of electric models and slows the switch to zero-emission light commercial vehicles.

A matching change is proposed to a separate EU regulation, Regulation (EU) 2019/2144, so that the same electric N2 vehicles in this weight range are also exempt from the speed limiter requirement under that regulation. The two changes are part of a wider package, the Automotive Omnibus, which aims to remove rules that place extra burdens on electric vehicles, particularly light commercial and small passenger cars. The proposal is intended to make electric delivery vehicles easier to adopt while keeping road safety and EU transport and climate goals in view.

posts.title: Simplification of technical requirements and testing procedures for motor vehicles (Omnibus IX on automotive)
posts.label: 🗳️ Lead committee adopted its report
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to revise and simplify the EU regulatory framework governing motor vehicles.
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: the automotive value chain is a pillar of the EU economy, accounting for EUR 589.3 billion and 3.7% of total value added of Europe’s GDP, and direct employment of 10.6 million Europeans. In an increasingly unpredictable trade environment, maintaining a robust and competitive automotive industry is essential for safeguarding the EU’s strategic autonomy and global economic standing. Representatives from the EU’s automotive industry have recently highlighted that a high number of legislations must be complied with by European vehicle manufacturers between now and 2030, resulting in up to 25% research & development costs in certain cases.
This proposal is part of the Automotive Omnibus which aims to remove regulatory barriers that disproportionately affect electric vehicles, in particular in the light commercial and small passenger car segments. It is implemented through two parallel legislative proposals: this proposed Regulation and a proposed Directive .
CONTENT: this proposal seeks to amend several key EU legislative acts governing motor vehicles in order to simplify technical requirements and testing procedures, reduce administrative burden, and improve regulatory coherence, while maintaining high levels of road safety, environmental protection, and market oversight.
More specifically, it amends Regulations (EC) No 561/2006, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2019/2144, and (EU) 2024/1257, with the objective of reducing unnecessary regulatory complexity, eliminating overlaps, and improving consistency across EU vehicle legislation. It seeks to make type-approval and compliance procedures more efficient for manufacturers and authorities, better reflecting technological progress and current market conditions.
Moreover, as part of this simplification effort, the proposal repeals Council Directive 70/157/EEC and Regulation (EU) No 540/2014, which contain outdated or redundant provisions, notably in the area of vehicle noise and technical standards. Their repeal contributes to greater legal clarity and consolidation of applicable rules within the updated regulatory framework.
The proposed Regulation concerns the following:
Removing regulatory obstacles for the uptake of electric light commercial vehicles
Electric light commercial vehicles are heavier as the result of the weight of their battery. An amendment allows Member States to exempt N2 e-vans - with a maximum authorised mass exceeding 3.5 tonnes but not exceeding 4.25 tonnes - engaged exclusively in domestic transport, from the obligation to install smart tachographs, in order to put them on equal footing with their fossil fuel equivalent, N1 diesel vans.
The main expected impact for the proposed measure is a reduced cost for companies, in particular SMEs that are the primary users/buyers of such vans, that will no longer have to install smart tachographs for the given type of e-van. In addition, the removal of the tachograph will also determine a reduction of administrative burden/costs for the companies/drivers who will no longer have to download tachograph data (2 to 4 hours a month). Moreover, levelling the playing field between N1 diesel vans and N2 e-vans through reduced prices for the latter will help stimulate the uptake of such e-vans.
In order to clarify the legal framework applicable to the specific case of motorhomes with a maximum authorized mass exceeding 7.5 tonnes used for private purposes, a second proposed amendment consists of allowing Member States to exempt motorhomes from the rules relating to driving times and rest periods, as well as the tachograph.
Accelerating the uptake of small affordable electric vehicles
The proposal establishes the legal basis for a new ‘small EV’ category , covering pure electric passenger cars below a defined length threshold. There is currently a lack of small affordable electric vehicles on the European market. In September 2025, the Commission President announced a small affordable car initiative aimed to incentivise the market for small electric vehicles. This will require targeted regulatory measures. The Commission will endeavour to freeze new requirements for 10 years and propose targeted incentives in the CO2 vehicle emission standards for small electric vehicles. The initiative may also lead to fiscal (such as subsidy schemes) and non-fiscal incentives (such as reserved parking space), compatible with State aid rules, where applicable. For this purpose, it is necessary to add a definition of a small electric car in motor vehicle legislation that can be used for targeted measures in EU legislation and by Member States. This would bring simplification for businesses, strengthen the business case to build small affordable electric cars profitably in Europe and reduce the price for consumers.
Simplifying the type-approval framework
With the increasing speed of innovation in the industry, in particular trends on automated driving and software updates, it is appropriate to assess the simplification potential in the EU type-approval framework for motor vehicles. Regulatory complexity can be a constraint for EU manufacturers in global competition with manufacturers from other jurisdictions. The proposal aligns EU type-approval requirements more closely with international standards, while expanding the Commission’s powers to adopt delegated acts on technical requirements for EVs.
The changes also aim to refer to ‘vehicle categories’ rather than ‘vehicle types’ for type approval of Euro 7 engines.
Reducing the adjustment costs related to Euro 7 emission tests
Annex V of the Euro 7 Regulation requires for the type-approval of heavy-duty vehicle engines tests per vehicle type. This requirement will introduce unnecessary administrative and regulatory burden by multiplying tests without providing additional environmental benefits. Therefore, the proposal streamlines emissions testing under the Euro 7 regime. It also provides for the development of on-board fuel consumption monitoring (OBFCM) devices and on-board monitoring (OBM) systems, as well as common methods for data processing.
Based on available information, it is expected that the amendments will result in significant annual savings of EUR 706 million for industry, including SMEs, citizens and public administrations.

aiSummaries.text:
This proposal is meant to simplify and update the EU's rules for motor vehicles, cutting red tape and removing overlaps while keeping road safety, environmental protection and market oversight in place. It amends several existing EU vehicle laws and repeals two older ones that contain outdated or duplicate rules, mainly on vehicle noise and technical standards. The European Parliament will decide on it together with the Council, on an equal footing.

The proposal is part of a wider package called the Automotive Omnibus, which aims to remove rules that make it harder for electric vehicles to compete, especially light commercial vehicles and small passenger cars. The EU's car industry is a major part of the economy, linked to about 10.6 million direct jobs, and industry representatives say the number of rules manufacturers must meet by 2030 is driving research and development costs up, in some cases by as much as 25%.

For electric light commercial vehicles, the proposal lets Member States exempt certain electric vans, those above 3.5 tonnes but not above 4.25 tonnes that are used only for domestic transport, from having to install smart tachographs. This is meant to put them on equal footing with comparable diesel vans, lowering costs for businesses, especially small ones, and cutting the time spent downloading tachograph data. It also lets Member States exempt private motorhomes over 7.5 tonnes from driving-time rules, rest-period rules and the tachograph requirement.

The proposal also creates a legal definition of a "small EV," a pure electric passenger car below a set length threshold, so that targeted measures can be applied to such cars. The aim is to encourage affordable small electric cars, which are currently scarce on the European market. Possible support includes incentives in CO2 standards, subsidies and non-financial benefits such as reserved parking, and the Commission would aim to freeze new requirements for these cars for 10 years.

Finally, the proposal simplifies the EU type-approval system, bringing it closer to international standards and widening the Commission's power to set technical requirements for electric vehicles. It also streamlines Euro 7 emissions testing for heavy-duty engines, so that tests are not repeated for every vehicle type without extra environmental benefit, and supports new on-board fuel consumption and monitoring systems. The proposal is expected to save industry, citizens and public administrations EUR 706 million a year.

posts.title: Clean corporate vehicles
posts.label: 🗳️ Lead committee adopted its report
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to accelerate the uptake of zero- and low-emission vehicles in corporate fleets, while fostering the competitiveness of the Union’s automotive sector.
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: corporate vehicles have a significant potential to accelerate the uptake of zero-emission vehicles (ZEV), due to their high share in new vehicle registrations (around 60% for new registration of cars and around 90% for new registration of vans) and their specific characteristics in terms of vehicle operations.
Due to the high share of corporate vehicles in new vehicle registrations, and their specific characteristics in terms of vehicle operations, measures targeting corporate vehicles have significant potential to accelerate the uptake of zero- and low-emission vehicles and the reduction of road transport emissions in the Union. However, that potential is currently underexploited. Corporate vehicles are responsible for a comparatively higher share of emissions compared to private vehicles, due to their generally higher yearly mileage, as is the case for example for some corporate fleets such as taxi and ride-hailing. A higher share of zero- and low-emission vehicles in those high-mileage fleets would result in high real-world fuel savings and emission reductions compared to current trends.
CONTENT: the proposed regulation establishes a framework for increasing the uptake of zero-and low-emission vehicles within the Union. It sets targets for the share of zero- and low emission vehicles in new corporate cars and vans registered by large undertakings in each Member State. This regulation does not prevent any Member State from setting more ambitious targets.
National targets
In view of the need to stimulate the market for zero- and low-emission vehicles while also supporting the further deployment of alternative fuels and leaving appropriate flexibility to Member States and market actors, the Commission has decided to set national targets. These targets will encourage Member States to put in place measures to incentivise the use of corporate zero- and low-emission vehicles by large companies . The design of the measures is at the discretion of each Member State . The resulting increase in the share of new zero- and low-emission vehicles in corporate fleets can help reduce road transport emissions faster, while increasing the availability of zero- and low- emission vehicles for citizens and businesses that rely on second-hand vehicles. These national targets are set at different levels of ambition for cars and vans in order to reflect the different levels of technology and market development, as well as the differences in targets for the respective vehicle categories under the CO2 emission performance standards. They are also differentiated between Member States in order to take account of the specific situation and characteristics of different Member States, in relation to their economy’s ability to address the higher initial capital costs of ZEV.
In respect the principle of technological neutrality, and to leave sufficient flexibility to the Member States, the proposal should set national targets that can be met through the combined share of zero- and low-emission vehicles.
The methodology to calculate those shares for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with the While the initiative introduces targets for Member States in the form of the share of new zero- and low-emission vehicles for large companies, the additional administrative burden for public authorities is kept to a minimum. The proposal builds on existing vehicle datasets and modalities that Member States already operate for vehicle registration and statistics, including business and fiscal statistics. While all Member States already have the necessary systems in place to identify new registrations of corporate vehicles, for distinguishing vehicle registered by SMEs or large companies in place, one-off administrative costs are expected.
SMEs are excluded from the scope of the proposal, which only targets new corporate vehicles registered by large companies (companies with at least 250 employees and EUR 50 million turnover), irrespective of their economic field of activity.
‘Made in the EU’
Since the transition towards zero-emission vehicles in corporate fleets may be subject to public financial support in Member States, there is a potential for using public support to help strengthen domestic value chains in the automotive sector.
Cars and vans ‘made in the European Union’ can contribute to the creation of a stable lead market for European suppliers, enhancing the competitiveness of Union industry, maintaining its workforce and helping attract new investments in Union production capacity in those sectors. To qualify for public financial support, vehicles will in the future have to be zero- or low-emission and manufactured in the EU. The Commission will rely on delegated acts to set up a methodology for determining the criteria for a car or van to be considered ‘made in EU’.

aiSummaries.text:
This proposed EU regulation aims to speed up the switch to zero- and low-emission vehicles in company fleets, while helping the EU's car industry stay competitive. The European Parliament and the Council would decide on it together, as equal partners.

The reasoning is that company vehicles are a large share of new registrations, about 60% of new cars and about 90% of new vans. They are also driven more miles per year than private cars, so they produce a disproportionate share of emissions. Shifting these high-mileage fleets to cleaner vehicles could bring real fuel savings and emission cuts sooner than current trends would.

To do this, the regulation sets national targets for the share of zero- and low-emission cars and vans that large companies register in each Member State. Each country decides for itself which measures to use to encourage this, and no country is prevented from setting more ambitious targets. The targets differ between cars and vans and between countries, reflecting differences in technology, market development, and each country's economic ability to cover the higher upfront cost of these vehicles. Countries can meet their targets using the combined share of zero- and low-emission vehicles, so they are not tied to one technology.

The regulation only covers large companies, defined as those with at least 250 employees and EUR 50 million in turnover. Small and medium-sized enterprises are excluded. The extra paperwork for public authorities should be small, since existing vehicle registration and statistics systems can mostly be used, though some one-off costs are expected to tell large and small company registrations apart.

The regulation also links public money to European manufacturing. In future, vehicles would have to be both zero- or low-emission and made in the EU to qualify for public financial support tied to this shift. The Commission will set the detailed rules for what counts as "made in the EU" later, through delegated acts. The aim is to build a stable home market for European suppliers, protect jobs, and attract investment in EU vehicle production.

posts.title: Amending certain production, labelling and certification rules and certain rules on trade with third countries
posts.label: 🤝 Lead committee approved the trilogue deal
posts.summary:
PURPOSE: to ensure fair competition and the proper functioning of the internal market in organic products, as well as ensuring consumer confidence in those products and in the organic production logo of the European Union.
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: organic farming is a key element of the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy with a growing share of land farmed organically and increasing consumer demand. The production and labelling of organic products are governed by Regulation (EU) 2018/848, applicable since January 2022, and the delegated and implementing Regulations which establish the detailed rules that underpin organic production.
The Court of Justice of the European Union concluded that neither terms referring to organic production nor the EU organic production logo may be used by products that comply only with standards merely equivalent to the production rules in Regulation (EU) 2018/848.
It is therefore necessary: (a) to ensure that consumers are able to make informed choices when purchasing products from third countries whose organic production and control systems have been recognised as equivalent to those of the Union, and (b) to ensure consumer confidence in those products and in the organic production logo of the European Union whilst ensuring fair competition within the internal market between products that fully comply with Union production and control rules and those that comply with rules equivalent to those Union rules.
Furthermore, given that the recognition of third countries whose organic production and control systems have been recognised as equivalent to those of the Union will expire on 31 December 2026, it is necessary and urgent for those third countries to continue to be recognised until 31 December 2036 to avoid disruptions in the trade of organic products.
Although the current legal framework is sound, targeted adjustments are deemed necessary to certain production rules to create a more efficient, effective, and user-friendly regulatory framework.
CONTENT: the proposal amends certain existing provisions of Regulation (EU) 2018/848 in order to: (i) facilitate organic production, labelling, controls and trade across the EU and in third countries; (ii) also ensure that consumers are able to make informed choices when buying organic products imported from third countries.
The proposal amends specific aspects of a limited number of provisions in Regulation (EU) 2018/848:
(i) it allows operators to use the products and substances available on the market for cleaning and disinfection for use in processing and storage ;
(ii) it adapts rules on labelling of organic products imported from third countries. This amendment ensures that consumers are able to make informed choices when purchasing products from third countries whose organic production and control systems have been recognised as equivalent to those of the Union;
(iii) it adapts the conditions for the exemption of smaller operators who sell unpacked organic products other than feed from the obligation of being in possession of a certificate. This amendment facilitates the exemption of smaller operators and therefore facilitates the achievement of the objective of encouraging short distribution channels and local production in the various areas of the Union;
(iv) it adapts and simplifies the requirements for the composition of groups of operators which will facilitate the implementation of the existing provisions and the development of organic farming;
(v) it postpones until 31 December 2036 the expiry of the recognition of equivalent third countries. This amendment avoids any disruption in the trade of organic products and ensures a smooth transition to the scheme of recognition of third countries through international agreements;
(vi) it adapts production rules for livestock by simplifying the current rules and adapt them to the needs of the operators.
Several elements in the proposal contribute to simplification, reducing bureaucracy and administrative burden for organic operators and Member States’ administrations.
The Commission estimates that these elements may entail annual direct administrative cost savings for a total of EUR 47.8 million , of which EUR 45.9 million for businesses and EUR 1.9 million for administrations. In addition, these elements may entail for businesses direct one-off adjustment cost savings of EUR 109.2 million and annual direct adjustment cost savings of EUR 90.2 million.
posts.whatsNext: The deal is provisional: it still needs a plenary vote in Parliament and formal adoption by the Council. Although confirmation is expected, either institution can still decline.

aiSummaries.text:
This proposal is a change to the EU's rules on organic products. Its goals are to keep competition fair within the EU market, to make sure shoppers can trust organic products and the EU organic logo, and to help shoppers make informed choices about organic products imported from outside the EU. It would be a regulation decided by the European Parliament and the Council on an equal footing, under the ordinary legislative procedure.

The current organic rules, Regulation (EU) 2018/848, have applied since January 2022. The EU Court of Justice has ruled that products may only use organic terms or the EU organic logo if they meet the full production rules in that regulation, not merely rules that are equivalent to them. The proposal also notes that the recognition of third countries whose organic systems are equivalent to the EU's will expire on 31 December 2026. It therefore asks that this recognition continue until 31 December 2036, so that trade in organic products is not disrupted.

The proposal changes several specific parts of the existing rules. It lets operators use cleaning and disinfection products available on the market when processing and storing organic goods. It adjusts labelling rules for organic products imported from third countries so that consumers can clearly see which ones are recognised as equivalent. It makes it easier for smaller operators who sell unpacked organic products, other than feed, to be exempt from holding a certificate, which supports short supply chains and local production. It simplifies the rules for forming groups of operators, and it simplifies the livestock production rules so they better fit what operators need.

According to the Commission's estimates, these changes could save businesses and administrations money. They could cut annual direct administrative costs by a total of EUR 47.8 million, of which EUR 45.9 million would be for businesses and EUR 1.9 million for administrations. For businesses, they could also bring one-off adjustment cost savings of EUR 109.2 million and annual direct adjustment cost savings of EUR 90.2 million.

posts.title: Defence readiness and facilitating defence investments and conditions for the defence industry (Omnibus V)
posts.label: 📜 Published in the Official Journal
posts.summaryLabel: Legislative Observatory, Decision by Parliament, 1st reading
posts.whatsNext: It's law. It enters into force on the date it specifies or, if none, the 20th day after publication in the Official Journal.

aiSummaries.text:
The European Parliament approved a regulation, by 530 votes in favour, 125 against and 12 abstentions, that changes several existing EU rules to make it easier for Europe to prepare its defence and for its defence industry to grow. It is part of a wider package of defence readiness measures and extends existing provisions from defence and non-defence laws to remove obstacles to defence investment.

The measure adjusts the European Defence Fund so that it helps the EU reach defence readiness by 2030, strengthening its strategic autonomy and resilience against a wide range of threats, including hybrid operations and the risk of armed aggression. The Fund is also meant to make the EU's defence industrial base more resilient, including by developing technologies that save energy and reduce reliance on outside suppliers for critical raw materials, and to encourage cooperation that matches the defence priorities agreed by Member States.

Paperwork for taking part in the Fund is to be reduced and procedures simplified. Small and medium-sized businesses and small mid-cap companies, especially those working across borders, should have fair access to funding calls, and the application and evaluation steps for calls involving them must be much shorter and simpler.

The Fund can also support disruptive defence technologies and research carried out by small and medium-sized businesses. Each proposal is judged on its contribution to excellence in defence, meaning its results must offer clear advantages over existing products or technologies, and on the quality and efficiency of how it would be carried out. Depending on the specific call, proposals may also be assessed on innovation, competitiveness, reducing dependence on non-EU sources, cross-border cooperation, efficiency over a product's life, further integration of the European defence industry, and meeting the needs of countries most exposed to conventional military threats.

Projects linked to permanent structured cooperation or to a structure for European armament programmes can receive a funding rate 10 percentage points higher. Finally, testing carried out in Ukraine, an EU candidate country, will be eligible for Fund support to strengthen cooperation with Ukrainian organisations.

posts.title: Acceleration of permit-granting for defence readiness projects (Omnibus V)
posts.label: 📜 Published in the Official Journal
posts.summary:
The European Parliament adopted by 540 votes to 105, with 22 abstentions, a legislative resolution on the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the acceleration of permit-granting for defence readiness projects.
The proposed regulation establishes common rules for the acceleration of permit-granting processes for defence readiness projects . Member States should determine which projects qualify as a defence readiness project under this regulation.
The European Parliament adopted its position at first reading by amending the Commission's proposal as follows:
Single point of contact
No later than 3 months after the date of entry into force of the regulation, each Member State should establish a single contact point as the sole contact point for the project in matters of defence readiness. The single point of contact should be the sole point of contact for a defence readiness project. At the request of the project promoter, prior to the permit application, the single point of contact should also provide information on the permit-granting process, including the documentation to be submitted as part of the application and the requirements under which a project could be considered a defence readiness project under this Regulation. The provision of such information should not prejudge the decision of the competent authorities to determine whether a project qualifies as a defence readiness project.
The Commission should assist the authorities of that Member State with capacity building in support of implementation of this regulation, in particular with technical assistance in establishing or operating a single point of contact and an interoperable portal.
Completeness check of the permit application
No later than 14 working days from receiving the permit application, the single point of contact should inform the applicant whether the permit application received is complete. If information is missing from the permit application, the single point of contact should request the project promoter to submit the missing information, specifying which information is missing.
If the submitted permit application is deemed to be incomplete for a second time, the single point of contact may, within 10 working days of the second submission, make a second and final request for information. If the submitted permit application is deemed incomplete for a third time, the process should be considered terminated.
Duration of the permit-granting process
The permit-granting process, including the granting of the relevant permit, should not exceed 42 working days from the date on which the single point of contact notifies the project promoter that it has received a complete permit application.
The competent authority may extend the time limit twice, up to a maximum of 60 working days , where:
- the exceptional nature, complexity, location, or size of the project so requires; or
- the defence readiness project raises exceptional risks to the health and safety of workers or the general population, or an exceptional environmental risk, and additional time is necessary to adequately assess those risks.
The total duration of the permit-granting process should not exceed 102 working days .
Any extension of the time limit should be notified in writing by the single point of contact to the project promoter within reasonable time before the expiry of that time limit. That notification should include the substantiated explanation of the reasons for the extension and the expected date of the comprehensive decision.
Where the single point of contact does not inform the project promoter of the outcome of the permit-granting process within 42 days or, where applicable, the extended time limit, the permits covered by the application should be deemed to be granted .
Where permits are deemed to be granted, the single point of contact should within eight working days of the expiry of the 42-day or, where applicable, 102-day period inform the project promoter and, where relevant, specify the conditions and requirements to which those permits are subject. Permits deemed to be granted may be challenged by affected parties.
Member States may, within 12 months after the entry into force of this regulation, provide that tacit approval should not apply in strictly limited and exceptional cases. A decision not to apply tacit approval should be made only following a case‑by‑case assessment, where the competent authority demonstrates, on the basis of duly substantiated and verifiable evidence, that the specific project raises a grave risk to human health or national security. In such cases, the Commission must be informed no later than one month before the entry into force of the national provision.
The individual decision to disregard tacit approval must be made and notified before the expiry of the 42 or 102 day period.
Monitoring, reporting, evaluation
Each Member State should submit to the Commission, annually , a statistical report on the application of this regulation, including the total number of permit applications granted, including those granted tacitly. Member States should inform the Commission about specific measures adopted to encourage and facilitate the participation of SMEs in defence readiness projects.
No later than 31 December 31, and every four years thereafter, the Commission should carry out an evaluation of the implementation of the regulation.

aiSummaries.text:
This measure sets common EU rules to speed up the permit process for defence readiness projects. Each country decides which projects qualify under the rules. The European Parliament adopted its position by 540 votes to 105, with 22 abstentions, after amending the Commission's original proposal.

Each country must set up a single contact point within 3 months of the regulation entering into force. This office is the only point of contact for a project. Before an application is filed, it can explain the permit process, the documents needed, and the conditions a project must meet to count as a defence readiness project. Giving this information does not decide whether a project qualifies. The Commission can help countries build this capacity, including technical support for setting up the contact point and an interoperable portal.

Within 14 working days of receiving an application, the contact point must tell the applicant whether it is complete and, if not, which information is missing. If an application is still incomplete after a second submission, the contact point can make one final request for information within 10 working days. If it is incomplete a third time, the process ends.

The permit process, including the decision to grant the permit, should take no more than 42 working days from the point the contact point confirms the application is complete. The deadline can be extended twice, up to 60 working days, if the project's exceptional nature, complexity, location or size requires it, or if it poses exceptional risks to health, safety or the environment that need more time to assess. The total process should never exceed 102 working days. Any extension must be notified in writing, with reasons and an expected decision date.

If the contact point does not give a decision by the 42-day deadline or the extended deadline, the permits are deemed granted. The contact point must then inform the applicant within eight working days and state any conditions attached. Affected parties can still challenge permits deemed granted. Within 12 months of the regulation entering into force, countries may rule out this automatic approval in strictly limited cases, but only after a case-by-case assessment shows, with solid evidence, a grave risk to human health or national security. The Commission must be told at least one month before such a national rule takes effect, and any decision to disregard automatic approval must be made and communicated before the deadline expires.

Finally, each country must send the Commission a yearly statistical report on how the regulation is applied, including the number of permits granted, including those granted automatically. Countries must also report on steps taken to help small and medium-sized enterprises take part in these projects. The Commission will evaluate how the regulation is working every four years, starting by 31 December.
